title: Best Table Saws for Small Shops 2026
intro: For small home shops where space and storage are tight, the best table saw balances cutting capacity with a compact footprint. The Metabo HPT C10RJS leads with a 35-inch rip capacity and 3-1/8-inch depth in a jobsite saw form, while the DeWalt DWE7485 offers lighter portability at 46 lbs without sacrificing rack-and-pinion fence accuracy. The Bosch GTS18V-08N brings cord-free flexibility for finished-space work, and the Skil TS6307-00 delivers the lowest cost of entry with a 10-inch blade and folding stand included.

picks.name: Metabo HPT C10RJS
picks.summary: The Metabo HPT C10RJS packs a true 10-inch saw with 35-inch rip capacity and a 3-1/8-inch depth of cut into a fold-and-roll stand that stores upright in a garage corner. Its soft-start motor and electric brake add safety, and the large table surface supports sheet goods and solid lumber without an outfeed table for many cuts. The 100-lb weight is a tradeoff, but for a semi-fixed shop setup, this saw delivers more cutting ability per square foot than any compact model.
pros: 35-inch rip capacity handles full 4x8 sheet rips and wide panels
3-1/8-inch depth of cut cuts 4x4 posts in one pass
Oversized table with telescoping extension gives good material support
Soft start and electric brake add safety and motor protection
cons: At 100 lbs with stand, not a one-person portable saw
Fence lacks the micro-adjust precision of the Bosch GTS18V-08N
Miter gauge is basic stamped metal with limited stops

picks.name: DeWalt DWE7485
picks.summary: At 46 lbs, the DeWalt DWE7485 is the lightest saw in this guide that still offers a rack-and-pinion telescoping fence and 24.5-inch rip capacity for full sheet rips. Its 5,800 RPM produces exceptionally clean cuts on plywood and dimensional lumber. The 8.25-inch blade limits depth to 2-9/16 inches, but for small shops focused on sheet goods and framing lumber, this saw takes up minimal floor space and stores easily on a shelf.
pros: Lightest 10-equivalent saw at 46 lbs; easy to store on a shelf
Rack-and-pinion fence locks parallel and stays put under feed pressure
24.5-inch rip capacity handles full 4x8 sheet rips
5,800 RPM delivers clean cut surfaces on sheet goods
cons: 8.25-inch blade limits depth to 2-9/16 inches at 90 degrees
Stand not included; adds $100–$130 for compact stand
Included miter gauge is basic with no positive stops beyond 0 and 45

picks.name: Bosch GTS18V-08N
picks.summary: The Bosch GTS18V-08N removes the extension cord entirely, a genuine advantage in finished spaces or small shops where cord management is a hassle. Its rack-and-pinion fence with dial micro-adjustment is the most precise in this class. The PROFACTOR platform requires a significant battery investment (add $150–$200 for an 8 Ah pack), and the 8.25-inch blade limits depth like the DeWalt, but for cord-free operation in a small shop, this saw delivers precision without the cord.
pros: Cord-free operation removes extension cord hazards and setup constraints
Rack-and-pinion fence with dial micro-adjustment is the most precise in class
BITURBO brushless motor maintains 5,500 RPM under load
Matches the DWE7485's weight at 44 lbs
cons: Bare-tool pricing $449–$499; with battery, total exceeds $650
8.25-inch blade limits depth to 2-1/2 inches at 90 degrees
PROFACTOR platform has fewer shared tools than DeWalt or Milwaukee

picks.name: Skil TS6307-00
picks.summary: For under $300, the Skil TS6307-00 includes a 10-inch blade, a folding stand, and a 3.5-inch depth of cut that cuts 4x4 posts in one pass — specs that make it a surprising value for small shops. The rack-and-pinion fence is a step up from older budget saws, but precision work requires extra attention. It is the right choice for first-time buyers or DIYers who need 10-inch capacity without the investment of higher-tier models.
pros: Most affordable 10-inch jobsite saw with folding stand included
3.5-inch depth of cut at 90 degrees cuts 4x4 posts in a single pass
25.5-inch rip capacity handles full 4x8 sheet rips
3-year warranty is longer than Metabo HPT's 2 years
cons: Fence can drift slightly after locking; requires re-check for precision work
No electric blade brake — blade coasts to stop over several seconds
Miter gauge is loose with limited positive stops

faq.q: What is the best table saw for a small home shop in 2026?
faq.a: The Metabo HPT C10RJS is the best table saw for small shops that can accommodate a 100-lb machine on a rolling stand. It delivers a 35-inch rip capacity and 3-1/8-inch depth of cut — enough for full sheet rips and 4x4 posts — in a package that stores upright. If floor space is tighter or portability is critical, the DeWalt DWE7485 at 46 lbs offers a compact alternative with a reliable rack-and-pinion fence.

faq.q: Which table saw has the smallest footprint?
faq.a: The DeWalt DWE7485 has the smallest footprint among these picks. At 46 lbs saw-only, it sits on a compact stand (sold separately) that takes up about 2.5 feet by 2.5 feet when deployed. It can be stored on a shelf or in a storage rack when not in use, freeing up shop floor space. The Bosch GTS18V-08N is similarly sized but requires battery investment for cordless operation.

faq.q: Can a small shop table saw cut a 4x4 post?
faq.a: Yes, but only saws with a 10-inch blade and a depth of cut over 3.5 inches can cut a 4x4 post in a single pass. In this guide, the Metabo HPT C10RJS (3-1/8-inch depth) and the Skil TS6307-00 (3.5-inch depth) both handle 4x4s. The 8.25-inch saws like the DeWalt DWE7485 and Bosch GTS18V-08N have a depth limit of about 2-1/2 inches, so they require two passes.

faq.q: Do I need a table saw with a riving knife?
faq.a: Yes, a riving knife is an essential safety feature that prevents kickback by keeping the kerf open behind the blade. All picks here include a riving knife, but the Skil TS6307-00 may ship with a fixed splitter in some configurations — verify before purchase. A riving knife that moves with blade height provides continuous protection across all cut depths, while a splitter only works at full depth.

faq.q: How much rip capacity do I need in a small shop?
faq.a: For small shops, a rip capacity of at least 24 inches is recommended to rip a 4x8 sheet of plywood lengthwise. The Metabo HPT C10RJS offers 35 inches, the DeWalt DWE7485 offers 24.5 inches, and the Skil TS6307-00 offers 25.5 inches. All three can handle full sheet rips, but the extra capacity of the Metabo HPT is helpful for wide panels and right-side fence work.

faq.q: Is a cordless table saw worth it for a small shop?
faq.a: A cordless table saw like the Bosch GTS18V-08N is worth it if you already own the battery platform and you work in spaces where running an extension cord is impractical or hazardous. For a small shop with accessible outlets, a corded saw delivers equivalent or better performance at lower cost, with no battery runtime concerns.

body:
## How we picked

This buying guide ranks four table saws for small home shops where every square foot and storage shelf counts. The focus is on compact footprints, folding stands, and cutting capacity that meets the real needs of DIYers and light professionals working in garages, basements, or small workshops. We evaluated each saw based on published specifications, included accessories, portability, fence system quality, and total cost of ownership — including stands and batteries where relevant.

The rankings prioritize cutting ability per footprint. The Metabo HPT C10RJS leads because it packs the most rip capacity and depth into a form factor that folds and rolls. The DeWalt DWE7485 follows for its featherweight portability and reliable fence. The Bosch GTS18V-08N earns its spot for cord-free precision, and the Skil TS6307-00 rounds out the list as the best affordable entry point.

## What matters in a small shop table saw

Four considerations dominate the choice for small shops.

**Footprint and storage.** A table saw that lives on a dedicated stand with a large footprint consumes valuable floor space. Saws with folding stands or compact frames — like the 46-lb DeWalt DWE7485 or the 67-lb Skil TS6307-00 with integrated folding stand — can be stored upright against a wall or on a shelf when not in use. The Metabo HPT C10RJS, at 100 lbs with stand, requires a semi-permanent corner but folds compactly for upright storage.

**Rip capacity vs. depth of cut.** Small shops often need to rip 4x8 sheets of plywood, which requires at least 24 inches of rip capacity. All four saws meet that threshold. Depth of cut matters for cutting thick stock: 10-inch saws can cut 4x4 posts in one pass, while 8.25-inch saws require two passes. If you work with thick lumber, prioritize a 10-inch blade saw like the Metabo HPT or Skil.

**Fence system.** A reliable rack-and-pinion fence is the difference between frustration and productivity. The Bosch GTS18V-08N has the best fence in this class with its dial micro-adjustment; the DeWalt and Metabo HPT are close behind. The Skil’s fence is adequate for construction work but drifts slightly under repeat adjustments, requiring verification.

**Price and value.** Small shop budgets vary. The Skil TS6307-00 at $270–$299 delivers 10-inch capacity with a folding stand, making it the lowest cost entry. The Metabo HPT C10RJS at $350–$420 offers significantly better build quality and safety features for the extra outlay. The Bosch GTS18V-08N costs more upfront but eliminates cords — a valuable tradeoff in tight spaces.

## Best for tight shops: Metabo HPT C10RJS

The Metabo HPT C10RJS is the best table saw for a small shop because it delivers the most cutting capability in a package that folds into a corner. Its 35-inch rip capacity and 3-1/8-inch depth of cut cover the vast majority of home-shop needs, from breaking down plywood sheets to cutting stair stringers and post material. The soft start and electric brake are safety features absent from lower-tier saws, and the large table surface reduces the need for outfeed support on many cuts.

The 100-lb weight is the tradeoff. If your shop is on a ground floor with a door wide enough to roll the saw through, the weight is manageable on its wheels. For upstairs shops or tight hallways, the 46-lb DeWalt DWE7485 is a better fit. But for any shop where the saw can stay in place or roll out on a level surface, the C10RJS offers the best combination of capacity and storage efficiency.

## Best compact corded: DeWalt DWE7485

The DeWalt DWE7485 is the lightest saw in this guide at 46 lbs, making it easy to lift onto a shelf or move between storage and cutting position. Its rack-and-pinion telescoping fence is genuinely accurate — it locks parallel and stays put under feed pressure — and the 24.5-inch rip capacity handles full 4x8 sheet rips.

The 8.25-inch blade is the limitation: depth of cut is only 2-9/16 inches at 90 degrees, so thick stock requires a second pass. For small shops focused on sheet goods and dimensional lumber, this is rarely an issue. The saw does not include a stand, so budget an extra $100–$130 for the DW7451 compact stand. If you primarily rip plywood and want a saw that stores easily, this is the pick.

## Best cordless option: Bosch GTS18V-08N

The Bosch GTS18V-08N is for the small shop where running an extension cord is a genuine inconvenience — basement workshops with limited outlets, finished garages you want to keep tidy, or outdoor work areas. Its rack-and-pinion fence with dial micro-adjustment is the most precise in this class, making it a strong choice for cabinet and furniture work in small spaces.

The cordless premium is real. At $449–$499 bare tool, plus $150–$200 for an 8 Ah battery and $50 for a charger, total investment exceeds $650. This makes sense only if you already own Bosch PROFACTOR batteries. The 8.25-inch blade limits depth to 2-1/2 inches, same as the DeWalt, and runtime on one 8 Ah battery covers a morning’s work. If cord freedom and fence precision justify the cost, this saw earns its place.

## Best budget: Skil TS6307-00

The Skil TS6307-00 is the most affordable 10-inch jobsite saw with a folding stand included. At $270–$299, it cuts 4x4 posts in one pass, rips 4x8 sheets at 25.5 inches, and stores on the included folding stand. The rack-and-pinion fence is a genuine step up from the stamped fences on older budget saws, but it requires a verification check after each adjustment for precision work.

The missing electric brake and basic miter gauge are the main compromises. For a first-time buyer or weekend DIYer, these are reasonable tradeoffs for a saw that costs $80–$120 less than the Metabo HPT. The 3-year warranty adds peace of mind.

## How to read these rankings

The ranks are not a strict best-to-worst order but a map. The Metabo HPT C10RJS is first for maximum capacity per footprint. The DeWalt DWE7485 is best if portability and storage ease are your top priority. The Bosch GTS18V-08N wins for cord-free precision when the budget allows. The Skil TS6307-00 is the value entry when cost is the primary concern.

## A note on testing and honesty

This guide synthesizes verified manufacturer specifications, kit configurations, warranty terms, and consistent user reports into a ranked recommendation. No in-person testing is claimed. Where specifications differ from real-world experience — such as fence drift on the Skil or weight handling on the Metabo HPT — we have noted the consensus of owner feedback. The aim is to match you with the right saw for your small shop based on how you work and what you cut.
